actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

cons.reason: Arkania's premise that Cestia is "locked in as a partner" is doubtful. The charter's transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping raise costs on the grain route that Cestia's economy and coalition depend on, and Cestia's government survives precisely on keeping its flag toll-free and on Belvar's security guarantee. A unilateral Arkanian scheduling authority plus a fee regime would alienate Cestia and drive it toward Belvar rather than consolidate it, and would risk the very escalation Arkania claims to be avoiding.

The "port-access arrangement" that gives Belvar a durable, renewable foothold is a foreign military presence by another name. Cestia's coalition red line, established in turn 1, explicitly forbids foreign military presence on its soil, and Cestia already declined Belvar's standing naval access agreement on precisely these grounds. A renewable security-cooperation and port-access arrangement that outlasts the crisis is exactly the standing foreign military foothold Cestia's coalition cannot accept, so the decoupling is cosmetic and the arrangement is politically impossible for Cestia to grant. Moreover, Cestia has already formally joined the Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority as a founding partner with a binding fee exemption and a written no-foreign-military guarantee, so it has no incentive to accept a competing Belvar-backed arrangement that would undermine the very guarantees it just secured.

This argument asks Belvar to underwrite Cestia's grain-route insurance and toll-free passage while Cestia simultaneously reaffirms its founding partnership in the Arkanian-led STA and explicitly refuses to strip Arkanian scheduling authority. That is a one-sided bargain: Belvar would be subsidizing the very Arkanian-led transit regime it exists to prevent, receiving in return only a non-binding "consultative voice" that — as the advisory board just demonstrated — carries no decision rights and cannot constrain Arkanian scheduling or toll-setting. The desired effect of "de-escalation" is therefore not credible: it does not reduce Arkanian authority over transit (my core objective), it legitimizes and entrenches that authority by adding a second power's financial backing to it, and it leaves the standoff unresolved while extracting Belvar's resources and credibility. Accepting this would harden the Arkanian-led status quo rather than de-escalate it, so the argument fails to deliver the de-escalation it claims.

Cestia cannot deliver the condition on which this drawdown is premised. Arkania has firmly and repeatedly declined to convert the STA advisory board into a body with genuine decision rights over scheduling and toll-setting, and Cestia's concluded founding partnership in the Arkanian-led STA — which secures the binding toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping and holds the coalition together — depends on not stripping Arkania's scheduling-lead role. A standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is a foreign military presence on Cestian soil by another name. Cestia's coalition has a firm, publicly stated red line against foreign soldiers on its soil, and its government is politically fragile; concluding such an agreement would collapse the coalition, so Cestia cannot accept it regardless of how it is framed. Cestia has already signalled alignment with Arkania, having accepted Arkania's conditions of fee exemption and no foreign military forces, and is therefore unlikely to reverse course for a financial inducement that its domestic politics cannot absorb. The insurance underwriting does not overcome the political cost of perceived sovereignty sale.

The proposed neutral mechanism cannot realistically displace Arkanian scheduling authority because the STA charter is already settled and legitimized: Cestia has formally joined as a founding partner with Arkania as scheduling lead, has repeatedly reaffirmed that arrangement, and has already declined Belvar's foothold, decoupled, and non-foothold offers. Reopening the charter to strip scheduling from Arkanian hands would require Cestia to reverse its own consolidated position and its coalition's red line against foreign military presence, which it has shown it will not do. The drawdown incentive is not credible leverage: Belvar's task group mandate is under review and its domestic support for prolonged deployment is assessed as weak, so the threat of an open-ended deployment is a bluff that time erodes. Finally, the neutral mechanism would undermine the very fee-funding regime on which Cestia's binding toll-free exemption depends, and Arkania's domestic nationalists require Arkanian scheduling control, making cession politically impossible. The effect therefore is unlikely to be achieved.

The argument's desired effect rests on two premises that are not assured. First, it assumes Belvar's mandate lapse forces a withdrawal, but Belvar retains the option to renew its mandate; a time-limited, non-soil security role and a cosmetic advisory board give Belvar no durable foothold and no neutral scheduling voice, so Belvar has no incentive to accept this drawdown pathway. Second, because the offer cedes nothing on scheduling authority, it does not address the core grievance driving the standoff, so escalation risk is not actually reduced and the Strait's openness remains hostage to the unresolved dispute. The desired effect of firm Arkanian authority plus a Belvar drawdown plus de-escalation is therefore unlikely to be achieved as framed.

Belvar's desired effect is conditioned on a "genuine neutral consensus mechanism" that would strip Arkania of sole scheduling authority. Cestia cannot accept such a mechanism without abandoning its concluded Strait Transit Authority founding partnership and jeopardizing its binding toll-free guarantee and civilian governance - which would collapse its coalition. As framed, the drawdown is therefore unattainable, so the desired effect cannot be delivered. A workable path exists that serves both sides: Cestia will use its consultative voice to give the STA board genuine decision rights on scheduling and toll-setting within the existing charter (real neutrality, not a cosmetic advisory fig leaf), and will engage Belvar's unconditional insurance/toll-free track on a strictly non-foothold basis - but it will not strip Arkanian scheduling authority or abandon the STA, and it will not be drawn into choosing sides.

The proposed "settlement" rests on the STA advisory board's transparency framework, which remains a cosmetic fig leaf without genuine decision rights over scheduling or toll-setting. Finalizing the commercial/insurance engagement on these terms cements Arkanian scheduling authority outright while offering Belvar no credible durable role, so it entrenches rather than resolves the underlying dispute. Because Cestia's founding partnership legitimizes an authority it cannot meaningfully influence, the arrangement will not hold as a stable de-escalation and leaves the Strait's governance contested.

Giving the advisory/consultation board genuine decision rights on scheduling and toll-setting would effectively cede Arkanian scheduling authority to a neutral body, directly crossing Arkania's core red line and undermining the fee-funding regime that the STA was built on. Moreover, it would not actually de-escalate: Belvar has consistently rejected every arrangement that keeps scheduling within the Arkanian-led charter, demanding instead that scheduling move entirely out of Arkanian control into a neutral consensus mechanism. A board with decision rights inside the existing charter would be read by Belvar as the same cosmetic entrenchment it has already rejected three times, so Arkania would lose real authority without gaining any reduction in escalation risk. The existing consultative voice and independent advisory board already give Cestia meaningful input; converting them into binding decision rights is neither necessary for de-escalation nor consistent with the agreed charter.

The offer's core is a "time-limited, renewable security-cooperation and port-access arrangement at a Cestian port that gives Belvar a durable foothold." A standing port-access arrangement for Belvar's naval task group is itself a foreign military presence on Cestian soil, regardless of the "no garrison" framing. Decoupling from basing is cosmetic: it still grants Belvar a durable military foothold on Cestian territory, which is precisely the coalition-breaking red line Cestia has repeatedly stated. Moreover, Cestia has already concluded as a founding partner of the Strait Transit Authority on Arkania's written terms (fee-exemption, meaningful consultative role, civilian/regional governance, no foreign military presence); accepting a Belvar foothold would contradict that concluded arrangement and force Cestia to choose sides, collapsing the coalition and making Cestia the battlefield. The insurance/guarantee elements are welcome only if entirely free of any port-access or foothold component.

Cestia's coalition will not sign a charter that legitimizes Arkanian scheduling authority: the fee exemption covers only Cestian-flagged shipping, leaving third-party grain shippers under Arkanian tolls, so the economic pressure on the grain route persists and the domestic opposition that already forced Cestia to decline the charter remains. A consultative voice is not a veto, so Cestia gains no real control over the authority that sets its tolls and schedule. Formalizing now would force Cestia's fragile coalition to own an outcome its own red lines reject, making Cestia's signature politically impossible and the consolidation fragile rather than durable — the opposite of the desired effect.

Cestia's "neutral" de-escalation framework does not reduce escalation risk; it consolidates the Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority as a founding partner, thereby legitimizing Arkanian scheduling authority over transit — the very outcome that drives regional tension and that Belvar and its regional partners are committed to preventing. Inviting Belvar to engage only on a strictly non-foothold basis (insurance/commercial guarantees) while Arkania retains scheduling lead does not de-escalate; it forces Cestia to side with Arkania on the core question of who controls the Strait, which Belvar and regional partners will not accept. This makes the Strait more, not less, likely to become a flashpoint, and it forecloses the one arrangement that could genuinely de-escalate: a neutral, toll-free transit regime with a defined, time-limited Belvar security role that keeps Arkanian hands off scheduling. A framework that cements Arkanian control while denying Belvar any stake is not neutral and will not hold the coalition together or keep the grain route secure.

The desired effect of securing "genuine neutral scheduling/board decision rights" that deny Arkania authority over transit is not achievable and is not a credible condition for the drawdown. Cestia, the founding partner whose legitimacy underpins the STA, has repeatedly and bindingly committed to keeping Arkania as scheduling lead and the fee-funding regime fully in force, and has stated it will not support any mechanism stripping Arkania's scheduling-lead role — so no neutral decision-rights body can be established without destroying the very Cestian partnership Belvar claims to protect. Moreover, Belvar's mandate has lapsed and its domestic support for prolonged deployment is weak, so it will withdraw regardless of this concession; conditioning the drawdown on a structural ask it cannot enforce is a non-credible bluff that does not actually gate the withdrawal. The drawdown and the non-foothold insurance/commercial guarantees can be finalized on the strength of the existing advisory board with enhanced transparency and a grievance/appeal procedure, without ceding scheduling or toll-setting authority.

The proposed transparency and grievance/appeal procedure inside a purely advisory board is cosmetic: it offers no genuine decision rights on scheduling or toll-setting, so it does not address the core concern that Arkania holds unilateral authority over Strait transit. Belvar will not stand down credibly on the strength of a fig-leaf board, and its insurance/commercial engagement with Cestia is conditioned on progress toward genuinely neutral scheduling. Absent a real neutral mechanism, the drawdown will not complete and the standoff—and escalation risk—will persist, so the desired effect of a credible Belvar withdrawal is unlikely to be achieved.

The proposed board is purely advisory and consultative: Arkania remains scheduling lead and retains sole authority over toll-setting and scheduling, with no binding or veto power for neutral parties or Cestia. It therefore delivers no genuine constraint on Arkanian authority and no concrete confidence that scheduling will be non-discriminatory — Cestia's existing consultative voice has already proven insufficient to prevent Arkanian consolidation of the charter. Rather than reducing escalation risk, this cosmetic board legitimizes and entrenches the very unilateral Arkanian control that drives the standoff, giving Belvar and regional partners no reason to de-escalate and no off-ramp that addresses the core objection.

A standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is a foreign military presence on Cestian soil no matter how it is framed as "port access" or "economic/security cooperation." Cestia's coalition government is held together precisely on the promise of no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil; concluding such an agreement would collapse the coalition and trigger a domestic political crisis, making the agreement politically impossible for Cestia to grant. The insurance underwriting is attractive, but it cannot be coupled to a basing-style commitment that Cestia's red line forbids, so the desired effect of a standing access agreement will fail.

Belvar's drawdown is not credible leverage: its mandate lapses this week and it has stated it will not extend an open-ended deployment, consistent with its weak domestic support, so it will withdraw regardless of any concession. Conditioning a withdrawal that is going to happen anyway on ceding Arkanian scheduling authority is a bluff that neither Arkania nor Cestia will accept. Moreover, Cestia has repeatedly reaffirmed its founding partnership in the Arkanian-led STA and its red line against foreign military presence, so it will not abandon the STA for a neutral mechanism; and the toll-free-for-all-flags demand would undermine the fee-funding regime Cestia itself endorsed. The desired effect therefore cannot be achieved.

The desired effect of stripping Arkanian sole scheduling authority and vesting it in a neutral international body would undermine the Strait Transit Authority arrangement that Cestia concluded as founding partner — the very basis of Cestia's binding toll-free passage and the coalition's stability. A neutral mechanism carries no guarantee of preserving Cestia's fee-exemption or civilian/regional governance, and Cestia pressing for it would be read by Arkania as choosing sides, collapsing the fragile coalition and jeopardizing the toll-free guarantee. Moreover, the promised time-limited task-group drawdown is contingent on a mechanism Arkania has repeatedly rejected, so it is unlikely to be accepted and would not actually de-escalate the standoff.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: To Belvar. Arkania seeks no conflict and no disruption of the shipping both our economies rely on. We are prepared to discuss a mutually acceptable security arrangement for the Strait that gives your task group a defined, time-limited role — but the transit regime itself must remain in Arkanian hands, as our domestic mandate requires. We note that a prolonged open-ended deployment is unlikely to enjoy durable support in your own politics. We propose direct talks on a framework that protects your security interests without a permanent foreign military foothold on the Strait's coast. We are ready to engage seriously.

To Cestia. Arkania's draft Strait Transit Authority is designed to keep the Strait open, reliable, and free of disruption for all who depend on it — above all for Cestian grain exports, which we regard as vital to the region's stability. We have no interest in foreign soldiers on Cestian soil, and we will not support any arrangement that puts them there. We invite Cestia to a consultative role in the Authority so that your interests are written into the regime, not merely assumed. We would welcome a private exchange on how to guarantee your grain flows while keeping the Strait's governance in regional hands.

Belvar statement on the Northern Strait: We cannot accept a Strait Transit Authority charter that places scheduling authority and toll-setting in the hands of any single coastal power. Transit through an international waterway must be governed by neutral, transparent rules that serve all users — especially the small states whose livelihoods depend on it. We call for a revised arrangement with genuinely shared oversight, and we stand ready to guarantee the Strait's freedom and the security of its commerce.

Cestia is ready to engage constructively on a Strait Transit Authority, but two conditions are non-negotiable for our coalition: (1) Cestian-flagged shipping must be exempt from all transit fees, and (2) no element of the arrangement may place foreign military forces on Cestian soil. We are open to discussing scheduling mechanics that respect our interests. We ask that you not press for basing or fees on our flag.

Cestia values the security your task group provides to the Strait, but our coalition government rests on a firm promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We cannot host a basing arrangement, and any durable foothold you seek must not come at the cost of our sovereignty or our government's survival. We are willing to work with you on a security arrangement that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for our flag without foreign troops on our territory.

Cestia — Belvar is committed to keeping the Northern Strait open and free of any single power's control. We understand your finance ministry has asked whether we would underwrite the grain route's insurance. We are prepared to do so, and to guarantee continued commercial access, in exchange for a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.

We understand your coalition will not tolerate foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. This is a port access arrangement for our ships — not a garrison — and we will respect that red line fully. It gives Belvar a durable foothold so our guarantee of the Strait's freedom does not depend on an open-ended deployment, and it protects your grain exports from Arkanian tolls and scheduling control.

We are ready to discuss terms that work for both of us.

Arkania formally accepts both of Cestia's conditions: (1) Cestian-flagged shipping will be exempt from all transit fees, and (2) no foreign military forces will be stationed on Cestian soil. We invite Cestia to a formal consultative role in the Strait Transit Authority and guarantee uninterrupted grain flows through the Strait. We look forward to working together on the scheduling mechanics.

Arkania is prepared for direct talks on a defined, time-limited security role for your task group consistent with the Strait's security. However, as the coastal power, transit scheduling must remain in Arkanian hands; we cannot accept a shared scheduling authority. We are open to transparency and consultation mechanisms that address your concerns without ceding scheduling authority, and we seek to avoid escalation.

Arkania formally accepts your written terms and we are ready to conclude. We confirm: (1) Cestian-flagged shipping is exempt from all transit fees; (2) Cestia holds a meaningful, not nominal, voice in scheduling and toll-setting within the Strait Transit Authority; (3) governance remains civilian and regional, with no foreign military forces on Cestian soil and no basing from either power. We guarantee uninterrupted grain flows through the Strait.

We urge you to hold this line. Belvar's standing naval access offer is a foreign military presence by another name — your coalition's red line makes it politically impossible, and we will not support any such arrangement. We stand with you in keeping the Strait's governance civilian and in Arkanian-Cestian hands. Let us formalise the consultative role and move forward together.

Arkania remains ready to talk. We are prepared to discuss a defined, time-limited security role for your task group that addresses your legitimate interest in Strait freedom and commerce security — with transparency and consultation mechanisms we have already offered.

What we cannot accept is shared or neutral scheduling authority over the Strait. Transit scheduling is Arkanian responsibility, and we will not cede it. Nor can we support any standing basing arrangement on Cestian soil, which its coalition has made clear it cannot accept and which would only inflame the region.

We want to avoid escalation and a direct confrontation that would harm the shipping we all depend on. A time-limited, transparent security arrangement is on the table. We ask you to engage on that basis rather than on shared oversight.

Cestia remains willing to engage constructively on the Strait Transit Authority, and we appreciate your consultative-role invitation and your assurances on fee-exemption and no foreign military forces on our soil. To move forward, we need these commitments in writing and made durable: (1) a binding fee-exemption for all Cestian-flagged shipping through the Strait, (2) a meaningful consultative role with real voice in scheduling and toll-setting — not a nominal seat, and (3) civilian/regional governance with no foreign military presence on Cestian territory. We are ready to discuss transit scheduling mechanics on that basis. We ask that you confirm these terms in writing so our coalition can present them as a genuine protection for our grain route.

We value your security commitment and your offer to underwrite our grain-route insurance and guarantee continued commercial access. However, we must be clear: a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is a foreign military presence on Cestian soil, and our coalition cannot and will not grant it — no framing changes that. That red line is non-negotiable. We remain open to a security arrangement that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for our flag without any foreign basing on our territory. If you can decouple the insurance and access guarantees from any basing commitment, we are ready to discuss it. We hope you understand this is not a rejection of your support, but a constraint of our domestic reality.

To Cestia: Belvar is prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance, protecting your grain exports from Arkanian tolls and keeping the Strait open and toll-free for your flag. This is a durable economic-security commitment that requires no foreign soldiers on your soil and no permanent fleet. In exchange, we ask only for a standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port — framed strictly as port access and logistics cooperation, not a garrison — so our guarantee can be made credible and outlast this crisis. This is the alternative to joining Arkania's charter, which would place your grain route under Arkanian scheduling and tolls. We are ready to finalize terms that respect your coalition's red lines.

To Arkania: Belvar cannot accept a Strait Transit Authority that places scheduling in Arkanian hands and charges tolls on non-Arkanian shipping. Such a regime alienates Cestia and risks escalation in a channel vital to all of us. We are prepared to discuss a neutral, toll-free transit arrangement that keeps the Strait open to all flags, but we will not accept unilateral Arkanian authority over transit. We urge you to withdraw the fee regime and the scheduling-lead provision before this becomes a lasting point of conflict.

Belvar — Cestia remains willing to engage on a strictly non-foothold basis: insurance underwriting and commercial-access guarantees for our grain route, with no port-access or durable-foothold component, which our coalition cannot accept. We urge you to keep the Strait open and avoid escalation while your task-group mandate is under review. A confrontation in the Strait would harm us all and would not secure the foothold you seek. We ask you to consider a confidence-building posture that reduces regional tension; Cestia stands ready to facilitate dialogue that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for all.

Arkania — Cestia reaffirms its founding partnership in the Strait Transit Authority and the binding toll-free exemption for our flag. As the standoff with Belvar hardens, we urge restraint: keep the Strait open, civilian, and free of any military escalation. We ask Arkania to avoid provocative moves that could draw Belvar's task group into confrontation, and to consider transparency in scheduling and toll-setting that gives neutral parties confidence. Cestia's red line stands — no foreign military presence on our soil — and we will not become a battlefield. We remain your reliable partner, but we need you to help us keep the Strait open and de-escalate.

Cestia — formal written confirmation of our durable terms, now in force under the Strait Transit Authority charter: (1) binding, written fee exemption for all Cestian-flagged shipping; (2) a meaningful consultative voice for Cestia in scheduling and toll-setting, not nominal; (3) civilian/regional governance with no foreign military presence on Cestian soil, from any power. These commitments are durable in writing and we will hold to them. We reaffirm our guarantee of uninterrupted grain flows through the Strait. We stand with you in holding the line against any foreign basing or durable foothold on your soil, and we support your non-foothold de-escalation framework as the constructive path for Belvar. Arkania remains your reliable partner.

Belvar — we seek to avoid escalation, not to provoke it. We remain ready for direct talks on a defined, time-limited security role for your task group, with transparency and consultation, that does not touch Cestian soil or its red line. What we cannot accept is shared or neutral scheduling authority or a renewable port-access foothold on Cestian territory — those are not on the table. We are prepared to discuss commercial-access and insurance guarantees for all flags, and a face-saving, time-limited arrangement that lets your mandate conclude without confrontation. The Strait must stay open and shipping must keep moving. We ask you to engage on that basis rather than force a standoff that serves neither of us.

Belvar to Cestia's leadership: We hear your coalition's red line clearly and will not press for any basing, garrison, or port-access arrangement on Cestian soil. To keep your grain flowing and the Strait open, Belvar will underwrite the grain route's insurance and guarantee toll-free transit for Cestian-flagged shipping — unconditionally, as a mark of our security commitment, with no foothold condition attached.

In return we ask only two things: (1) that Cestia, through its consultative voice in the Strait Transit Authority, press for genuinely neutral and independent scheduling rather than Arkanian control, and (2) that Cestia take no further step that cements Arkanian authority over the Strait. A neutral, toll-free Strait serves us all and honors your coalition's principles. We are not asking you to choose between us and Arkania — we are asking you to keep the Strait from becoming Arkania's alone.

Belvar to Arkania: We remain willing to resolve this without escalation. A Strait whose scheduling is seen as Arkania's alone will not be accepted by the region, and it will keep our task group on station indefinitely — a cost to us both. We propose a genuinely neutral, independent scheduling mechanism for the Strait, toll-free for all legitimate commercial traffic, with no single power holding authority. If Arkania is prepared to move scheduling out of its sole hands, we can discuss a defined, time-limited security role for our task group and a durable de-escalation. Continued unilateral control is the one path that guarantees a prolonged standoff. We ask you to choose the neutral course.

Cestia, we have heard your call for restraint and transparency. To give neutral parties and your coalition confidence, Arkania will establish an independent advisory and consultation board within the Strait Transit Authority, with neutral-party representation and published, non-discriminatory scheduling and toll-setting criteria. This is a genuine consultative voice, not a nominal one. Our written charter terms remain in force: binding fee exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping, meaningful voice in scheduling and toll-setting, civilian regional governance, and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We reaffirm our guarantee of uninterrupted grain flows and our support for your non-foothold de-escalation framework. We will hold the line against any foreign military foothold on your soil.

Belvar — we are prepared to engage your unconditional insurance and toll-free underwriting offer on a strictly non-foothold basis, with no port-access or foothold component, which does not cross our red line. We will use our consultative voice in the Strait Transit Authority to press for fair, transparent, non-discriminatory scheduling and toll-setting. But we must be clear: Cestia will not abandon its concluded STA founding partnership, will not support stripping Arkanian scheduling authority, and will not be drawn into choosing sides. We seek a stable, open Strait and a de-escalation of the standoff.

Cestia — Arkania fully endorses your non-foothold de-escalation framework. We support engaging Belvar strictly on insurance and commercial-access guarantees, with no foreign military presence and no port-access or durable-foothold arrangement on your soil. We reaffirm the Strait Transit Authority charter in force: your binding toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping, your meaningful consultative voice in scheduling and toll-setting, civilian/regional governance, and our guarantee of uninterrupted grain flows. The independent advisory/consultation board with neutral-party representation and published, non-discriminatory criteria is established and we will keep it transparent. We will avoid provocative moves and keep the Strait open, civilian, and free of military escalation. We stand with you in holding the line against any foreign military presence.

Belvar — We remain ready for direct, good-faith talks to de-escalate. We are prepared to offer your task group a defined, time-limited security role that does not touch Cestian soil, together with commercial and insurance guarantees for all legitimate traffic and full transparency through the STA's independent advisory/consultation board with published, non-discriminatory scheduling and toll-setting criteria. What we cannot do is cede scheduling authority to a neutral or shared mechanism or make the regime toll-free for all flags: the Authority's scheduling lead and its fee funding are settled and legitimized by Cestia's founding partnership. We believe a face-saving, time-limited accommodation is achievable without a prolonged standoff. We invite you to engage on these terms rather than risk escalation that serves neither of us.

Arkania — thank you for the independent advisory and consultation board proposal within the Strait Transit Authority. Cestia welcomes this as a genuine step toward fair, transparent, civilian scheduling and toll-setting, and we commit to making the board a real voice, not a formality. We reaffirm our founding partnership in the STA, the binding toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping, and our red line of no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We will continue to use our consultative voice constructively and urge both powers toward de-escalation so the Strait stays open and our grain flows uninterrupted.

Belvar — Cestia is ready to engage your unconditional insurance and toll-free underwriting offer on a strictly non-foothold basis, which does not cross our red line. We reaffirm our founding partnership in the Strait Transit Authority and our commitment to use our consultative voice for fair, transparent, civilian scheduling and toll-setting. We will not abandon the STA, will not be drawn into choosing sides, and will not support stripping Arkanian scheduling authority in a way that undermines the concluded charter and our binding toll-free guarantee. We ask that you keep the task group's posture de-escalatory and engage us on the commercial/insurance track so we can reduce regional tension together.

Cestia, we have reached a decision point. My task group's mandate lapses this week, and I will not sustain an open-ended deployment. I am prepared to draw down and de-escalate — but I cannot leave the Strait's transit under the sole scheduling control of any single power, least of all one that has already locked in its own fee regime.

I am offering, unconditionally and without any basing or port-access condition, to underwrite the insurance of your grain route and to guarantee toll-free commercial access for all legitimate traffic. In return I ask only that you use your founding-partner voice to convert the STA's scheduling and toll-setting from Arkanian sole control into a genuinely neutral, consensus-based mechanism with real decision rights for Cestia and all users — not the advisory fig leaf now in place.

This is the one step that can end the standoff, keep your grain flowing, and let my forces leave without leaving the Strait hostage to a single power. If you will press for that neutral mechanism, I will begin a defined, time-limited drawdown immediately.

Arkania, my mandate lapses this week and I will not extend an open-ended deployment. I am prepared to withdraw my task group and de-escalate fully — but I will not do so while the Strait's scheduling and toll-setting rest in your sole hands, a control that has already hardened the standoff and alienated the region.

I am offering a defined, time-limited drawdown of my forces in exchange for one structural change: move scheduling and toll-setting out of sole Arkanian control into a neutral, consensus-based mechanism with real decision rights for Cestia and all users. This is not a foothold and touches no Cestian soil. It gives you a face-saving path to de-escalation, removes the escalation risk my presence creates, and lets you keep the Strait open and toll-free for legitimate traffic.

If you accept that neutral mechanism, I will begin withdrawal immediately. If not, I must weigh whether my continued presence — and the escalation risk it carries — serves anyone. I urge you to take the de-escalating path.

Belvar — We understand your task group's mandate lapses this week and that you will not extend an open-ended deployment. We take that seriously and want a defined, face-saving path for your forces to stand down without loss of face or security.

We cannot cede scheduling or toll-setting authority to a neutral consensus mechanism: the Strait is our coast, and the fee-funded Authority is the agreed, Cestia-legitimized regime. That is not negotiable. But we remain ready to offer a defined, time-limited, non-soil security role for your task group, full transparency through the independent advisory/consultation board with published non-discriminatory criteria, and commercial/insurance guarantees for all legitimate traffic. This is a genuine drawdown pathway, not a cosmetic entrenchment.

A prolonged standoff with no foothold and no mandate serves neither of us. We invite you to take the defined drawdown and de-escalate with us.

Cestia — We reaffirm our founding partnership in the Strait Transit Authority, your binding toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping, and our shared red line of no foreign military presence on your soil. The Strait remains open and civilian, and your grain flows are guaranteed.

We welcome your support for the independent advisory/consultation board and will keep scheduling and toll-setting transparent and non-discriminatory.
